report:
**Conclusion:** Your answer is broadly right: ginkgo extract is not supported as a reliable treatment for tinnitus symptoms.

The strongest evidence is a Cochrane review of randomized trials (1,543 participants), which found **no evidence of benefit when tinnitus was the primary problem**. A later Cochrane update likewise judged the evidence on benefits and harms versus placebo **uncertain**, rather than demonstrating effectiveness—largely because trials are limited and outcomes vary.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36383762/

**Evidence against the conclusion:** Some trials and reviews of the particular standardized product EGb 761 have reported improved tinnitus ratings, especially in people who also had dementia or other neurosensory symptoms. But this is not persuasive evidence that it relieves primary tinnitus generally: those populations, formulations, comparisons, and outcome measures differ, and favorable findings have not changed systematic-review conclusions.  
https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0157574

A large placebo-controlled trial (over 1,100 people with stable tinnitus) is also part of the evidence base and found no convincing benefit.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC26593/

So, “no proven benefit” is more precise than “it definitely cannot help anyone.” Ginkgo can also interact with medicines—particularly drugs affecting bleeding—so discuss it with a clinician or pharmacist before trying it, especially if taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs.
